pages.name: No load
pages.task: The load is switched off. What voltage does the capacitor settle at?
pages.answer: 325 V, the peak of the humps
pages.why: It settles at 325 V, the peak. Each peak fills the capacitor until it matches the top of the hump. Then the diodes block. With no load, nothing drains it, so it stays there. It fills only from the supply, so it never passes the peak. A smoothing capacitor adds no voltage of its own.

pages.name: How far it falls
pages.task: The bus falls 2 V every millisecond. The humps come 100 times a second. Roughly how far does the bus fall between refills?
pages.why: About 20 V. The humps come every 10 ms. The bus falls for about that long, at 2 V a millisecond. That dip is the [[ripple]]. The refill starts a little before each peak. So the drawn dip is a little smaller, about 18 V.

pages.name: Double the load
pages.task: The load doubles to 4 A. The capacitor stays the same. What happens to the ripple?
pages.why: It doubles, to about 40 V. The bus falls at I ÷ C. Twice the current drains it twice as fast. So in the same 10 ms it falls twice as far. The capacitor does not set the ripple alone. The load and the ripple frequency set it too.

pages.name: An idle drive
pages.task: A 400 V drive stands idle, with its motor stopped. What does its DC link read?
pages.why: About 566 V, the peak. With no load, the capacitor fills to the peak and stays there. On 400 V that is 400 × √2 = 566 V. Under load it sags towards about 1.35 times the line voltage, 540 V. Both figures are right, each at its own load.

pages.name: Five time constants
pages.task: Precharge puts a 100 Ω resistor in the way. With 1000 µF, the time constant R × C is 0.1 s. By the charging curve, when is the capacitor about full?
pages.answer: After about 0.5 s, five time constants
pages.why: After about 0.5 s, five time constants. Each time constant closes 63% of the gap that is left. After five, only e^−5 of the gap is left, under 1%. So the capacitor is about 99.3% full.

pages.name: Keep the ripple
pages.task: The load grows to 4 A. What capacitance keeps the ripple at 10 V?
pages.why: 4000 µF. The ripple is I ÷ (f × C). Double I and the ripple doubles. Double C as well and it halves back. Check: 4 ÷ (100 × 0.004) = 10 V.

pages.name: Six-pulse ripple
pages.task: A six-pulse drive runs from 400 V, 50 Hz. Its DC link has 1000 µF, and the load takes 5 A. Roughly what ripple does the rule give?
pages.why: About 17 V. Six pulses a cycle on 50 Hz give a ripple frequency of 300 Hz. So the ripple is about 5 ÷ (300 × 0.001) = 17 V. That is a third of what a bridge gives with the same capacitor and load.
